faq.a: Propofol is preferred because it has minimal cardiovascular depression and does not worsen anaemia.
faq.q: What is the safest induction agent in a patient with malaria‑related anaemia?

faq.a: Ketamine increases sympathetic tone, which can precipitate dangerous blood pressure spikes.
faq.q: Why avoid ketamine in a hypertensive patient?

faq.a: Use a gum‑elastic bougie with a standard laryngoscope, maintain oxygenation with a mask, and have a surgical airway kit ready.

exam: What are the three most important pre‑induction assessments for a patient with sickle‑cell disease? — Airway exam, baseline haemoglobin/oxygenation, hydration status; optimise hydration and avoid hypoxia.

A 45‑year‑old male with active pulmonary TB needs emergency laparotomy. How does TB affect your anaesthetic plan? — Anticipate reduced lung compliance, use lung‑protective ventilation, avoid nitrous oxide (may worsen pulmonary hypertension).

During maintenance you notice a sudden rise in end‑tidal CO₂ and muscle rigidity. What is your immediate action? — Stop the volatile agent, hyperventilate with 100% O₂, give dantrolene if available; treat malignant hyperthermia.
Explain why succinylcholine is contraindicated in a patient with severe burns. — Burns cause up‑regulation of acetylcholine receptors leading to dangerous hyperkalaemia on depolarisation.
You have no capnography. How will you confirm correct endotracheal tube placement? — Observe chest rise, auscultate bilateral breath sounds, check for condensation, and monitor oxygen saturation.

A patient develops postoperative nausea and vomiting despite prophylaxis. What next step is appropriate? — Give a second‑line antiemetic such as dexamethasone or metoclopramide; consider non‑opioid analgesia.

Why is regional anaesthesia not always feasible in low‑resource settings for abdominal surgery? — Requires sterile technique, ultrasound or nerve stimulator, and trained staff; lack of these may increase failure or complications.

What are the key signs of inadequate ventilation during GA when capnography is unavailable? — Decreasing SpO₂, rising PaCO₂ (if arterial blood gas possible), absent chest movement, and increased work of breathing.
ai.title: General Anaesthesia
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: General anaesthesia renders a patient unconscious and insensate for surgery. In low‑resource settings the clinician must anticipate airway, drug and monitoring challenges and plan safe induction, maintenance and emergence.

b: Requires assessment of airway, comorbidities and fasting status before induction.
sections.p: A reversible drug‑induced state of unconsciousness, analgesia, amnesia and muscle relaxation that allows surgery without patient awareness.

b: Light: purposeful movement to stimulus; Moderate: purposeful movement to pain; Deep: no response, stable vitals.
sections.p: Depth is graded by clinical response and, where available, EEG‑derived indices (e.g., BIS). In low‑resource settings rely on verbal response, eyelash reflex and haemodynamic stability.

b: Major abdominal, thoracic or orthopaedic procedures
Patients with severe anxiety, seizures, or uncontrolled pain
Contraindication to regional techniques (coagulopathy, infection).
sections.p: The need for GA arises from surgical factors (duration, invasiveness) and patient factors (inability to cooperate, severe pain).

b: Airway assessment (Mallampati, neck mobility)
Baseline vitals and oxygen saturation
Review of medication list for interactions.
sections.p: Before induction the patient is awake, may be anxious, and may have comorbidities such as HIV, TB, malaria or sickle‑cell disease that affect drug choice and monitoring.
Basic pre‑operative labs guide drug selection and anticipate complications.

t.b: Detect anaemia, infection or thrombocytopenia; anaemia may require transfusion, infection may need antibiotics before surgery.
Identify electrolyte disturbances or renal impairment that alter drug metabolism; correct before induction.
Assess for active TB, pneumonia or cardiac enlargement; plan ventilation strategy.
Determine infection status for infection control and drug interaction risk; if unavailable, use universal precautions.

b: Difficult airway (Mallampati III‑IV, limited neck extension)
Severe hypotension after induction (hypovolaemia, myocardial disease)
Malignant hyperthermia susceptibility (family history, unexplained intra‑operative deaths)
Aspiration risk (full stomach, gastro‑oesophageal reflux).
sections.p: Complications can arise at any stage; early recognition saves lives.

b: Induction: IV propofol or thiopentone for rapid loss of consciousness; avoid ketamine in patients with uncontrolled hypertension.
Muscle relaxation: succinylcholine for rapid sequence intubation; avoid in patients with hyperkalaemia or burns.
Maintenance: volatile agent (halothane, isoflurane) if a vapouriser is present, otherwise total IV anaesthesia with propofol infusion.
Analgesia: IV fentanyl or morphine; avoid NSAIDs in renal failure or active bleeding.
Monitoring: pulse oximetry, non‑invasive BP, ECG, capnography if available; if capnography unavailable, watch for chest rise and auscultate breath sounds.
sections.p: Plan includes pre‑medication, induction, maintenance, monitoring and emergence, tailored to resources.

b: Observe for respiratory depression, nausea, wound infection.
Provide multimodal analgesia; consider regional block if feasible.
Educate patient on signs of infection and when to return.
sections.p: Post‑operative care focuses on airway protection, pain control and early detection of complications.

b: Spinal anaesthesia – produces sensory block below a level, patient remains awake.
Sedation – patient is drowsy but can respond to verbal commands.
sections.p: Local or regional anaesthesia, which provide analgesia without loss of consciousness.

b: Normal haemoglobin may mask chronic anaemia in sickle‑cell disease; assess functional status.
Normal ECG does not exclude occult coronary disease in diabetic patients; consider stress testing if time permits.
sections.p: Laboratory or clinical signs may appear normal despite underlying risk.

whenToSeekHelp: Cannot intubate or ventilate despite attempts
Severe hypotension unresponsive to fluids and vasopressors
Suspected malignant hyperthermia (rapid rise in temperature, rigidity, hypercarbia)
